sources.title: Florence Pugh (Wikipedia article, read 2026-10-04)
sources.speaker: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: Lead; Early life; Career (Early roles; Breakthrough); Public image; Personal life and other work; Accolades
sources.excerpt: Florence Pugh was born on 3 January 1996 in Oxford to dancer Deborah and restaurateur Clinton Pugh. She has three siblings: actor and musician Toby Sebastian, actress Arabella Gibbins, and Rafaela "Raffie" Pugh. She suffered from tracheomalacia (a windpipe condition causing breathing problems) as a child, which led to frequent hospitalisations. The family relocated to Manilva in Spain when Pugh was three years old, hoping the warmer weather would improve her health. They lived there until she was six, when they moved back to Oxford. [...] Zach Braff's drama film A Good Person (2023), in which Pugh starred as a car crash survivor, marked her first producing venture. Instead of opting for a wig, Pugh cut off her own hair for the part. [...] She insisted on filming the scene where Belova jumps from the top of Merdeka 118 without using stunt doubles. Marvel Studios was initially reluctant to allow Pugh to perform the stunt due to insurance concerns, but after her persistent efforts, including discussions with Kevin Feige, she was permitted to perform the jump. [...] From 2019 to 2022, Pugh was in a relationship with American actor and filmmaker Zach Braff. [...] She has been dating the British actor Finn Cole since 2024. Pugh has polycystic ovary syndrome and endometriosis.
sources.context: Tertiary summary used only for biographical scaffolding (birth, family, filmography, accolades, release slate). Fetched as plaintext via the MediaWiki API on 2026-10-04. The DWD "allegedly clashed with Wilde" sentence is an allegation and must not be relied on. Lists Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026) among her Yelena films and upcoming East of Eden, Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three. Not independent evidence of motive. Wikipedia's Merdeka 118/insurance sentence cites Variety, 2025-04-14 (now S62), which the edit stage opened; the article cites S62, not Wikipedia, for that detail.

sources.title: Florence Pugh Felt Acting Was a 'Massive Mistake' After Execs Criticized Her Body at 19: They Tried to Change the 'Shape of My Face'
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh, quoted from an interview with The Telegraph; article by Zack Sharf (Variety)
sources.locator: Article body, paragraphs 2-6
sources.excerpt: “I felt very lucky and grateful, and couldn’t believe that I had got this top-of-the-game job,” [...] “All the things that they were trying to change about me – whether it was my weight, my look, the shape of my face, the shape of my eyebrows – that was so not what I wanted to do, or the industry I wanted to work in,” Pugh said. “I’d thought the film business would be like [my experience of making] ‘The Falling,’ but actually, this was what the top of the game looked like, and I felt I’d made a massive mistake.” [...] “That made me fall back in love with cinema – the kind of cinema that was a space where you could be opinionated, and loud, and I’ve stuck by that,” Pugh said. “I think it’s far too easy for people in this industry to push you left and right. And I was lucky enough to discover when I was 19 what kind of a performer I wanted to be.”
sources.context: Relay of a Telegraph interview given during The Wonder press (late October 2022). Telegraph original is not reachable from this environment and was not opened. The pilot was Fox's Studio City (rising pop star opposite Eric McCormack); Fox passed on it, she returned to England, and the Lady Macbeth audition came 'two weeks later'. Note she did not refuse the changes: the show died. The 'stuck by that' resolution is retrospective self-report from six to seven years later. S03 relays the same interview and is not independent.

sources.title: How To Hit A Grand Slam: Florence Pugh On Her Breakout Year (Deadline Q&A)
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh, interviewed by Anthony D’Alessandro (Deadline)
sources.locator: Intro paragraph; answers on Fighting with My Family, Midsommar (Dani) and Little Women
sources.excerpt: Pugh got Aster and Gerwig to work it out a schedule so that she could walk from one film to the next. [Deadline narration] [...] Ever since Lady Macbeth and Family, I’ve been going back-to-back for about four years now. [...] In all honesty, I was scared, because I’d never come close to any sort of grief like that in my entire life. I didn’t know what that looked like, I didn’t know what that sounded like, and in a film where that is heavily based around anxiety and grief, it would almost be rude to wing it. [...] I imagined every single member of my family in a coffin, which got all the noises that you see in the film out of me. I’m sure many actors would say that’s totally ridiculous, but unfortunately, I can’t cry on cue. So, I had to really just destroy myself for an entire three months, but I was happy with the work. [...] Coming off Midsommar, Amy March in Little Women was the best therapy for me. She was amazing. I got to prance around in petticoats, and essentially flirt with Timothée Chalamet every day, and then punch and wrestle with all the sisters. It was great. [...] I've watched it twice and every time, I've come out of it feeling completely hungover, and just dead.
sources.context: Awards-season Q&A at the end of her 2019 breakout year. The earliest and least hindsight-shaped account of the Midsommar method; predates her 2023-2025 'abuse' framing. Deadline's own narration says 'Pugh got Aster and Gerwig to work it out a schedule so that she could walk from one film to the next' (writer's words). Opened in full; verified verbatim. Edit stage (2026-10-04) re-read the cached page: the schedule narration, 'I was scared' and 'completely hungover, and just dead' are verbatim.

sources.title: The Louis Theroux Podcast S6 E6: Florence Pugh (machine transcript)
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh, in conversation with Louis Theroux
sources.locator: Transcript timestamps 00:09:14-00:12:45 (arguing with directors; crying-scene retakes); 00:17:00-00:20:10 (Midsommar, Little Women, depression); 00:36:22-00:36:59 (being heard); 00:46:06-00:49:30 (privacy, Braff); 00:50:25-00:52:40 (past relationship, people-pleasing)
sources.excerpt: “sometimes at the beginning of my career, I hadn't quite figured out the relationship between director and actor yet, and I found myself arguing a lot. I mean, it's something that I still do in a softer way now [...] I just always felt so protective of the character that I was playing” / “women on set um it's a bit stickier you can't really be a problem because people will say that you're a nightmare [...] and when I'm in that state I kind of I'm a bit mushy so I'm like okay we'll do it again And my co-star went up to the director and said, don't do that, man. [...] I wouldn't have been able to have said that because that wouldn't have been received well.” / “Little Women was such a fun experience [...] so I think shelled all of that and then when I got home for Christmas I was so depressed I was like oh I think that's from Midsama and I didn't deal with it” / “I think when you're such a when you're such a bubbly person and you fill in a lot of energy for other people it's definitely I'm definitely the last person that I look after [...] I needed to be upbeat for everybody else and my issues, my worries, my pains weren't worthy of being spoken about. They weren't necessary to speak about because it would bring people down and we don't want that. [...] it's that people pleaser thing where you just try and keep things afloat without anybody else knowing that you're paddling for dear life.” / “I stood up for it and I stood up for him and I stood up for me just being allowed to do whatever the fuck I wanted to do [...] the one thing I can do is stop talking about that part of my life.”
sources.context: Long-form, unhurried conversation (about an hour), the most reflective source in the record. Machine transcript without speaker labels; the quoted lines are first-person answers and two segments were cross-checked against official YouTube clips by a research sub-agent. Do NOT attribute the ambiguous 'would you ever say no... no way can't do that' exchange near 00:11:11 to her. 'Shelled' is the transcript's rendering (likely 'shelved'). The people-pleasing passage follows her account of an unnamed past relationship that was 'causing you pain'; do not identify the partner. Opened and spot-verified verbatim. SUPERSEDED for quotation by S63: the edit stage checked the episode audio itself. The audio confirms this transcript's 'upbeat', 'it would bring people down', the 'people pleaser... paddling for dear life' sentence and the 'arguing a lot... in a softer way now' lines; it also contains 'good for everybody else' immediately before 'upbeat', so the print relay (S58) and this transcript each captured half of the sentence.

sources.title: On the Eve of East of Eden, Florence Pugh Talks About Her Year of Rest and Relaxation (Vanity Fair cover story, October 2026 issue)
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh, interviewed by Hillary Busis; with testimony from Zoe Kazan, Denis Villeneuve, Ari Aster, Ashley Park, Andrew Garfield, David Harbour
sources.locator: Full text; sections on Cathy Ames; Midsommar and protecting her space; siblings; Venice/Don’t Worry Darling; Finn Cole; social media; Gaza; producing and sets; lateness and rest
sources.excerpt: “I don’t know how to play characters without sympathizing with them. And I think I’ve tried to do my best after Midsommar to be fair to myself and also to be fair to the character,” she says. “I’ve learned over the years to know when enough is enough, when I’ve abused my state of mind or put my body through things that I shouldn’t. I now know how to protect my space.” [...] “I don’t like messy sets,” she says. “I want people to come to work and work, and enjoy that it’s a luxury to do this. When moods change on set, it’s because someone is preventing that from happening, and that’s what makes people feel like they haven’t been cared for.” [...] “I know that everybody in this industry has rises and falls. I’m not an idiot,” [...] “I wasn’t healthy, I wasn’t happy,” she says. “And I remember at the end of the year going, ‘Eww. I really want to change that. That’s not me.’” [...] “You don’t like that behavior? Change it now before it becomes comfortable.” [...] “I love packing,” she says. “I hate unpacking.” [...] “I don’t want to be a secret, but I also don’t want everything to be divulged,” [...] “But no, I was never scared of it”—even if she estimates she lost hundreds of thousands of followers for posting about the topic. [...] “I want to enter this decade and be like, We’re not gonna coast. We’re not gonna stay the same.” [...] “One of the things that I find most interesting about Florence is that she’s so lovely and warm and approachable and funny,” Kazan tells me. “And at the same time, she’s kind of all business on set. I walked away from our process not understanding any better than I did beforehand how she works.” [...] “There is something unapologetic about the way she inspires respect,” Denis Villeneuve, director of the Dune trilogy, says via email. [...] 'Pugh hasn't publicly told her side of the story, and that is not going to change today. "Oh, no. I feel like there's so much stuff we've covered that is important for me and on track with my life and my career," she says when I bring up the film.' [...] 'this year, she realized what she wanted most was to stay home, tend her garden, host her friends, nuzzle her dog, not live out of a suitcase. It's a break that will allow her to enjoy everything she enjoys and avoid one activity she doesn't. "I love packing," she says. "I hate unpacking."' [...] 'This new adaptation will debut in October'
sources.context: Most recent long-form interview (conducted in London, July 2026, per research sub-agent; published online 2026-09-25 for the October 2026 'New Establishment' issue). Also contains: 'Oh, no. I feel like there's so much stuff we've covered...' when asked about Don't Worry Darling; asked how she met Finn Cole: 'No.'; 'I don't have that tic anymore. I guess maybe I'm not addicted to it anymore'; Ashley Park: 'She's a great chef, she's a great host, she's a great designer, she's a great planner. She has a confidence that's not egotistical'; Harbour: 'She gave me a lava lamp?'; on Cathy: 'I thought it was the most beautiful love letter to protecting her as a child. When I read that, I was like, ‘I can get behind her.’'; 'Emma Thomas, Amy Pascal. I gravitate toward women that command space.' The 'doesn't care about being adored by strangers' and 'control the narrative... without coming off as controlling' lines are the writer's interpretation. Opened directly in full via curl and verified verbatim. Edit stage re-read the cached full text on 2026-10-04 for the packing context, the 2026 Don't Worry Darling deflection and the October debut.

sources.title: Florence Pugh Says 'Instagram Censored Me' Over Cornell 7 Posts Addressing Sexual Assault Case
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh on The View; article by Zack Sharf (Variety)
sources.locator: Article body: Sara Haines question and Pugh answers; quoted Instagram posts
sources.excerpt: “Rape is something that lives. The fear of it lives in our bodies, and when stories like this come out and it’s really not picked up in the way that you hope it’s picked up, it makes me feel scared, it makes me feel anxious, it made me feel so much rage,” Pugh answered. “I’m lucky enough to do what I do and I have a platform and I wanted to talk about it.” [...] “I’m able to come here and talk about it in real life, even though, sadly, Instagram censored me when I said it, which is also just another shock that women are censored, even when they go through these things, they can’t talk about it,” [...] Pugh added her in second post: “Instagram decided to block my post from getting in front of the right people. Tut tut tut. Oh dear. That doesn’t look great does it? Here’s another go at it in case you were one of those people that can no longer see my post.” [...] originally posted about the Cornell University sexual assault case in an Instagram post that the social media platform covered with a content warning that read: 'This post contains content that some people may find upsetting.' Pugh put up a second post calling out Instagram for 'blocking' her statement. [...] 'It's an ongoing conversation and it will always be an ongoing conversation until we're harder on those that do that to women.'

claims.claim: In December 2019 she told Deadline: 'unfortunately, I can't cry on cue. So, I had to really just destroy myself for an entire three months, but I was happy with the work.'

claims.inference: Consistent account across 2019 (Deadline, TheWrap) and 2025 (Theroux). Shows willingness to enter pain deliberately for the work.
claims.alternative: This is professional method under a director's demand, not a life choice about her own pain; it complicates any claim that she avoids pain. Shoot length is given as 'three months' (2019) and 'like four months' (2023).

claims.alternative: Do not present the illness as a formative wound or causal origin of her temperament; she rejects that reading and no source supports it. The voice is a physical trait, not a personality signal.

claims.claim: She told Vogue in 2023: 'I never want this to be a sob story, because it's never been a story in my life.'
claims.passage: "I never want this to be a sob story," she told Vogue in 2023, "because it's never been a story in my life."
claims.inference: She explicitly refuses a wound narrative; the article draws nothing about type from the illness.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Vogue 2020: 'Pugh grew up in a family of hosts' (restaurateur father, grandfather who ran a pub).
claims.passage: Vogue described "a family of hosts" in 2020
claims.inference: Hosting is a learned family practice, which weakens collaborators' hosting praise as evidence of a Two motive.
claims.alternative: A learned practice can still express a motive; the self-reports carry the Two case.

claims.claim: Of a childhood school nativity she told The Guardian (2018): 'It was the first time I knew the power of being on stage... I have complete control.' I still feel that now.'
claims.passage: "It was the first time I knew the power of being on stage. I remember thinking, 'Oh God, they're waiting for me, they're listening to everything I say and I have complete control.' I still feel that now,"
claims.inference: A consistent, vivid early pleasure in performance, in holding a room and in the 'power' and 'control' of an audience's attention.
claims.alternative: Childhood performers of every type say this. 'Power' and 'complete control' fit Type 8 or Type 3 as well as Type 7. The BBC Radio 4 versions (S43) are machine-transcribed and are not quoted.

claims.claim: The Observer, December 2014 (age 18): 'Throughout my life, I've been that annoying kid on every stage at school, in every talent contest.'
claims.passage: At 18 she called herself "that annoying kid on every stage at school, in every talent contest."
claims.inference: Early, pre-fame self-description as a compulsive performer.
claims.alternative: Self-deprecating interview humour.

claims.claim: The childhood performance record does not discriminate between Types 7, 8 and 3.
claims.passage: "Complete control" sounds as much like an Eight, or a Three holding an audience, as a Seven chasing the thrill of the live moment.
claims.inference: Honest limit on the childhood evidence.
claims.alternative: None; this is a statement of what the evidence cannot show.

claims.claim: At 17 she nearly did not send a tape for The Falling's open audition because of what her brother's career had taught her ('that's not how you're going to get a part'); her mother persuaded her ('it's kind of a free go'), and she was cast.
claims.passage: "My brother was in the industry, and I knew that's not how you're going to get a part, handing in a three-minute tape." Her mother talked her into it: "We know you aren't going to get it, but this is something you want to do with your life, so it's kind of a free go."
claims.inference: A protective pessimism about hope followed by full commitment once in the room. Director Carol Morley says she 'quickly knew she was Abbie'.
claims.alternative: Accounts of the route in differ: tape at home (S49, S43), leaflet at school (S46), the agent emailing schools (S47), or Morley visiting her boarding school (S45). Treat the details as approximate; the hesitancy rests on retrospective self-report.

claims.claim: The Observer, December 2014: 'I do like a bit of danger... Guns, cars, running, bullets. I'm up for it.'
claims.passage: "I do like a bit of danger," she told The Observer. "Guns, cars, running, bullets. I'm up for it."
claims.inference: Thrill-seeking predates the stunt record (C13, C14) by a decade.
claims.alternative: Light, genre-preference remarks by a teenager promoting an art film; useful only as a pattern marker.

claims.claim: The Observer, December 2014: 'It's a bit of a fluke.' She repeated the worry in 2017 and 2022.
claims.passage: And of her break: "It's a bit of a fluke."
claims.inference: Recurring self-doubt under the confident persona, consistent with her own statement that confidence came later (C36).
claims.alternative: Modesty is a British interview norm, and calling an early break a fluke is a common humility move; it may also reflect a Type 6 or Type 3 worry. Not decisive.

claims.claim: In 2022 she told The Telegraph (via Variety) that the Studio City pilot's makers tried to change 'my weight, my look, the shape of my face, the shape of my eyebrows'.
claims.passage: that the people behind the pilot tried to change "my weight, my look, the shape of my face, the shape of my eyebrows,"
claims.inference: A retrospective origin story (told in 2022) that frames her later stance as a refusal to be reshaped. The pilot was not picked up; she did not have to refuse anything at the time.
claims.alternative: First told in 2018 (S44), retold in more detail in 2022; her only account from the moment (S46, April 2015) is eager. The later framing is retrospective, not brand-era invention.

claims.claim: Told 2022 (via Variety): 'I think it's far too easy for people in this industry to push you left and right.'
claims.passage: "it's far too easy for people in this industry to push you left and right."
claims.inference: States the value of not being pushed around, which Sevens and Eights share.
claims.alternative: Retrospective framing three to seven years after the event; first told in 2018 (S44).

claims.claim: Grazia, April 2017 (age 21): 'I don't like being told how to do things... it makes Katherine angry, and it made me angry.'
claims.passage: "I don't like being told how to do things," she told Grazia in 2017, describing scenes where the men around her _Lady Macbeth_ character confine her: "it makes Katherine angry, and it made me angry."
claims.inference: Anti-constraint is her oldest stated value, voiced at 19 to 21 before her persona was a brand, and it lines up with her later 'push you left and right' and 'freedom' language (C04, C18).
claims.alternative: Resisting being told what to do fits Type 7 (freedom from limits) and Type 8 (autonomy, refusing control) about equally; the teenage-school context is ordinary adolescent friction.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her stated object of defiance (being told, pushed or reshaped) does not discriminate between Seven and Eight.
claims.passage: That is shared ground: Sevens resist being boxed in, and Eights resist being controlled.
claims.inference: Autonomy wording fits 7 and 8 about equally, so it is not used to tilt the call.
claims.alternative: Some readers treat freedom-from-limits as Seven-specific; this profile does not.

claims.claim: AP, July 2019: 'To get it perfect, I knew, would be so exhilarating and the payoff would be a fantastic feeling — which it was.'
claims.passage: "To get it perfect, I knew, would be so exhilarating and the payoff would be a fantastic feeling — which it was,"
claims.inference: A dated arc of reinterpretation, moving from thrill to cost to boundary. The thrill framing came first and the pain was named years later.
claims.alternative: The shift may reflect changing industry vocabulary about wellbeing and the incentives of later press cycles, not a change in her underlying pattern.

claims.claim: Off Menu podcast, March 2023 (via Variety): 'I think by the end I probably, most definitely abused my own self in order to get that performance.'
claims.passage: she said she "most definitely abused my own self in order to get that performance"
claims.inference: Middle step of the dated arc of reinterpretation (C07).
claims.alternative: Relay; podcast audio not reviewed. Comedy-podcast setting.

claims.claim: November 2025: 'But I don't do that anymore. It really fucked me up.'
claims.passage: "But I don't do that anymore. It really fucked me up."
claims.inference: Late step in the arc.
claims.alternative: Retrospective; therapeutic vocabulary common in recent press cycles.

claims.claim: At the Valentino couture show in Rome on 2022-07-08 she wore a sheer pink gown whose lining she and Pierpaolo Piccioli had removed.
claims.passage: On July 8, 2022, at Valentino's couture show in Rome, she wore a sheer pink gown
claims.inference: A deliberate choice, a forceful public reply mixing defiance and comic timing, and a stated 'mission' of not letting her body be reshaped by others' expectations (compare C04).
claims.alternative: The gown was a fashion-house moment with publicity value; defiance with humour fits 7 (sass, play) and 8 (confrontation). The caption original was not opened (relays match).

claims.claim: Instagram caption, July 2022: 'I was excited to wear it, not a wink of me was nervous.'
claims.passage: not a wink of me was nervous
claims.inference: First public response led with confidence.
claims.alternative: Instagram original not opened; TODAY relay matches PAPER and WWD per research notes.

claims.claim: Instagram caption, July 2022: 'Why are you so scared of breasts? ...'
claims.passage: "Why are you so scared of breasts?"
claims.inference: Defiance delivered as comedy.
claims.alternative: Instagram original not opened (relay).

claims.claim: British Vogue, September 2024, after the writer raised online commentary about her body: 'It's really painful to read people being nasty about my confidence or nasty about my weight. It never feels good.'
claims.passage: "It's really painful to read people being nasty about my confidence or nasty about my weight. It never feels good."
claims.inference: The first public response led with confidence and humour; the hurt was acknowledged two years later. Her chosen word for what critics fear is 'freedom'.
claims.alternative: Normal processing over time, and the 2024 setting (a reflective cover interview) invites vulnerability. This does not establish that she hid hurt in 2022.

claims.claim: Interpretation: in her public telling of Midsommar (2019 to 2025) and the Valentino dress (2022 to 2023-2024), the thrill or comeback came first and the hurt was named later.
claims.passage: In both episodes the thrill or the comeback led her telling and the hurt followed: about a year later for the dress, six years later for _Midsommar_.
claims.inference: A claim about the order of her public accounts, not proof that she concealed pain at the time.
claims.alternative: She named some cost early (2019 'scared', 'destroy myself'; the 2022 caption's harm to women); reflective cover interviews invite later admissions.

claims.claim: On the Theroux podcast (episode audio, about 00:48:44) she described 'a relationship that was causing you pain' without naming the partner.
claims.passage: Discussing a past relationship she has not named, one she described as "causing you pain,"
claims.inference: Context for C09: the people-pleasing passage arose from this relationship.
claims.alternative: Do not identify, date or sequence the partner; EW (S60) is not linked in the article.

claims.claim: Theroux episode audio (00:49:24-00:50:10): 'I'm definitely the last person that I look after ... I needed to be good for everybody else, I needed to be upbeat for everybody else and my issues, my worries, my pains weren't worthy of being spoken about ... because it would bring people down.'
claims.passage: "I think when you're such a bubbly person and you fill in a lot of energy for other people, ... I'm definitely the last person that I look after ... I needed to be good for everybody else, I needed to be upbeat for everybody else and my issues, my worries, my pains weren't worthy of being spoken about ... because it would bring people down."
claims.inference: Her most explicit description of a costly pattern: she hid pain because it would bring others down. The stated reason concerns the room's mood, not looking weak.
claims.alternative: A self-report about one painful period; ranking her needs below others' comfort is at least as consistent with Type 2 as Type 7.

claims.claim: Theroux episode audio (about 00:50:24-00:50:35): 'it's that people pleaser thing where you just try and keep things afloat without anybody else knowing that you're paddling for dear life.'
claims.passage: that people pleaser thing where you just try and keep things afloat without anybody else knowing that you're paddling for dear life
claims.inference: Verified in the audio by the edit stage; a self-description of concealment for others' sake.
claims.alternative: UNVERIFIED WORDING: appears only in an unlabelled machine transcript; no print relay found. The article flags this inline. Check audio before the edit stage keeps it.

claims.claim: The Daily Times relay (S58) prints 'good for everybody else' and omits 'upbeat'; the machine transcript (S17) has 'upbeat'; the audio (S63) has both.
claims.passage: Print write-ups tidied this passage and some dropped "upbeat"; the wording here is checked against the episode audio.
claims.inference: Tells readers where the wording comes from.
claims.alternative: Whisper transcription can mishear; three model passes agree on the quoted words.

claims.claim: Interpretation: in the Theroux passage her stated reason for hiding pain is others' mood, not fear of appearing weak.
claims.passage: The reason she gives for hiding pain concerns the room. Her pains "would bring people down." She says nothing here about looking weak.
claims.inference: Central to the 7-versus-8 discriminator.
claims.alternative: Limited to this passage; elsewhere she pre-empts shame by exposing herself first (S36), which is closer to an Eight's control of exposure.

claims.claim: In late March 2020, in lockdown in Los Angeles, she began 'Cooking with Flo' after her father asked 'Why aren't you dancing and why aren't you cooking?'
claims.inference: Coping by activity and pleasure.
claims.alternative: Instagram Story expired; secondary transcription only. Lockdown cooking was widespread.
claims.passage: "My dad called me yesterday and said, 'Why aren't you dancing and why aren't you cooking?' ... So this morning I woke up and I danced and I felt better and now I'm going to cook."

claims.claim: Instagram Story, March 2020: 'we have to do things that keep us happy, keep us bubbly and keep moving basically... Get all of the weird horrid anxiety out of your system.'
claims.passage: we have to do things that keep us happy, keep us bubbly and keep moving basically
claims.inference: Her stated coping recipe is activity, pleasure and lightness: dance, cook, keep moving. The cooking also serves others (feeding people) and family tradition (C31).
claims.alternative: Cooking during lockdown was widespread; the Story itself was not opened (secondary transcription). Food and hosting also fit a Type 2 reading.

claims.claim: Vogue 2023, of her teens: 'So many of the things that I did were quick fixes... Things were so wrong in my head... Oh, well, I can change my nails. Oh, I can buy an eyelash kit.'
claims.passage: "So many of the things that I did were quick fixes," she told Vogue in 2023.
claims.inference: Her account complicates collaborators' 'supernaturally confident' image: confidence was built over time, and her teenage coping was a run of quick fixes.
claims.alternative: 'Quick fixes' for teenage distress is common adolescent behaviour; resist over-reading.

claims.claim: Vogue 2023, of her teens: 'Things were so wrong in my head and things were so wrong with school life and things were so dark and scary. And so I would try and do quick things like, Oh, well, I can change my nails. Oh, I can buy an eyelash kit.'
claims.passage: "Things were so wrong in my head and things were so wrong with school life and things were so dark and scary. And so I would try and do quick things like, Oh, well, I can change my nails. Oh, I can buy an eyelash kit."
claims.inference: Concrete instance of C36.
claims.alternative: She is describing adolescent distress; ordinary teenage coping. No diagnosis is implied.

claims.claim: Who What Wear, May 2025, of the Merdeka 118 stunt: 'I could persuade myself to do that... I can basically pretend to myself not to listen to my instincts.'
claims.passage: I can basically pretend to myself not to listen to my instincts
claims.inference: Fear override; used only in the counterphobic-Six paragraph, not as Seven pain-to-pleasure evidence.
claims.alternative: Fits an Eight's denial of vulnerability or a counterphobic Six as well as a Seven.

claims.claim: Interpretation: convergent coping pattern across her teens, 2018-2019 and 2020, anchored on Midsommar.
claims.passage: Together, from her teens through 2020, with the _Midsommar_ sequence as the anchor, they suggest a pattern: distress met with movement, pleasure and a lighter register, with the reckoning afterward.
claims.inference: Built from C36, C08, C15, C14.
claims.alternative: Each item is weak alone (stated in the article); the strand rests mostly on retrospective self-report.

claims.claim: Cate Shortland (Vogue 2020): 'She is bloody scary. Steely. Absolutely will not back down. She has a healthy amount of anger in her as a person, at the injustices she sees around her.' Other collaborators converge (Gerwig, Johansson, Villeneuve).
claims.passage: "She is bloody scary. Steely. Absolutely will not back down. She has a healthy amount of anger in her as a person, at the injustices she sees around her."
claims.inference: Five independent named collaborators over seven years converge on strength, refusal to yield and anger at injustice. This is the core of the Type 8 case.
claims.alternative: All are promotional-cycle quotes about a star the speaker cast or co-starred with; they describe work presence. Shortland's comment is about stunts. Against them: her own 'mushy' on-set account (C23) and 'people pleaser' (C09).

claims.claim: Scarlett Johansson (Harper's Bazaar 2022): 'She's unapologetically herself.'
claims.passage: "She's unapologetically herself."
claims.inference: Named co-star testimony supporting the 8 case.
claims.alternative: Promotional quote.

claims.claim: Denis Villeneuve (Vanity Fair 2026, by email): 'There is something unapologetic about the way she inspires respect.'
claims.passage: "There is something unapologetic about the way she inspires respect."
claims.inference: Named director testimony supporting the 8 case.
claims.alternative: Promotional quote.

claims.claim: TheWrap, December 2019: 'I'm already a bit of a big mouth. I already love telling people what's what.'
claims.passage: "I'm already a bit of a big mouth. I already love telling people what's what."
claims.inference: A stable self-concept stated across three interviews over three years. 'Telling people what's what' is assertive; 'brightest thing' and 'loud and dramatic' read as expressive and attention-seeking in a playful register.
claims.alternative: Self-description in promotional interviews; expressive extraversion fits Type 7, 8, 3 or 2 equally. It establishes temperament, not motive.

claims.claim: The on-camera haircut in A Good Person was her idea, drawn (per Vogue 2023) from her own teenage experience of distress; Braff resisted before she persuaded him.
claims.passage: Cutting her own hair on camera in _A Good Person_ (2023) was her idea, drawn, Vogue reported, from her own distress as a teenager
claims.inference: Observable, repeated choices in which she overrode institutional caution. Two are framed in service of the character, one in service of the team.
claims.alternative: Physical transformation is rewarded by awards culture and press; Braff's testimony is not independent. Her stunt rationale ('we all got to do it') is collective, not self-aggrandising. Fits Type 8 (force of will) and Type 7 (thrill) alike.

claims.claim: Zach Braff (Collider 2023): 'And she just kept saying, You'll figure it out, you'll figure it out.'
claims.passage: "she just kept saying, 'You'll figure it out, you'll figure it out.'"
claims.inference: Named testimony of persistence.
claims.alternative: Not independent: former partner, promotional context.

claims.claim: Per her Fandango interview (relayed by Variety, 2025-04-14), Marvel balked at the Merdeka 118 jump over 'a crazy insurance ordeal' and she kept emailing Kevin Feige until it agreed: 'I had to keep on pushing.'
claims.passage: When Marvel balked at letting her do the Merdeka 118 skyscraper jump in _Thunderbolts*_ (2025) over "a crazy insurance ordeal," she told Fandango, she kept emailing Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige: "I had to keep on pushing."
claims.inference: Persistence against institutional caution (Eight-leaning), told gleefully ('wonders for the press tour').
claims.alternative: Promotional anecdote; her enjoyment of heights and the press-tour framing fit a Seven's thrill as well.

claims.claim: In April 2020 a birthday post for her then-partner Zach Braff (21 years older) drew abuse; she turned off comments for the first time and posted a video defending the relationship.
claims.passage: In April 2020, a birthday post for her then-partner Braff, 21 years older than her, drew so much abuse that she turned off comments for the first time.
claims.inference: She was willing to lose followers to defend a partner and her own autonomy. In hindsight she gives two motives: protecting him and freedom to choose.
claims.alternative: Fits Type 8 (protective confrontation), Type 2 (defending a loved one) and Type 7 (freedom). The draft avoids the clause on which relays disagree.

claims.claim: April 2020 video: 'please unfollow me because the abuse that you throw at him is abuse that you throw at me, and I don't want those followers.'
claims.passage: "please unfollow me because the abuse that you throw at him is abuse that you throw at me, and I don't want those followers."
claims.inference: Willingness to lose audience to defend a partner.
claims.alternative: Instagram original not opened; this clause matches across relays. In 2025 she said the abuse was only at him (S60).

claims.claim: At the Together for Palestine benefit in London in September 2025 she said: 'Silence in the face of such suffering is not neutrality, it is complicity.'
claims.passage: "Silence in the face of such suffering is not neutrality, it is complicity"
claims.inference: Repeated willingness to accept audience loss and platform friction for causes she sees as protecting the vulnerable; anger and teasing appear together.
claims.alternative: Activism aligns with her peer group; fits 8 and 2 more directly than 7.

claims.claim: Vanity Fair 2026: 'I was never scared of it'; she estimated she lost hundreds of thousands of followers over Gaza posts.
claims.passage: She told Vanity Fair in 2026, "I was never scared of it," and estimated she had lost hundreds of thousands of followers.
claims.inference: Cost tolerance for a cause.
claims.alternative: The follower figure is the writer's paraphrase of her estimate.

claims.passage: In late September 2026, after a former Cornell University student filed a civil lawsuit alleging a 2024 sexual assault, Pugh posted about the case. As of September 30, 2026, Variety reported, the case was pending and some of the accused denied wrongdoing.
claims.inference: Describes only her action and the case status.

claims.inference: Public moral anger paired with named fear and anxiety.

claims.inference: A deliberate move toward authorship and running sets. Her rationale for order on set is people's feeling of being cared for and of enjoying the work.

claims.review_trigger: Update if she announces a directing or writing debut or new producing deals, and phrase the East of Eden credit as completed once later seasons or projects are announced.

claims.claim: Discriminator 1a: concealing pain for others' sake separates her from Eight, not from Two.

claims.inference: Concealment for others' comfort is the Helper's move; it is not used as Seven evidence.
claims.alternative: One relationship-specific self-report.

claims.claim: Theroux (wire relay): for women on set it is 'a bit stickier' because they may be branded 'a nightmare'.
claims.passage: it can be "a bit stickier," in case they are called "a nightmare."
claims.inference: Her own circumstantial explanation for on-set softness.
claims.alternative: Fragments within the wire writer's paraphrase.

claims.claim: Theroux (wire relay): after about six takes of a crying scene the director wanted another; 'And when I'm in that state, I'm a bit mushy, so I'm like, Okay, we'll do it again.'
claims.passage: "And when I'm in that state, I'm a bit mushy, so I'm like, 'Okay, we'll do it again.'"
claims.inference: In the most concrete conflict anecdote in the record she did not refuse, and another person drew the line for her. Her stated motive for arguing is protecting the character, not winning.
claims.alternative: Key circumstantial counterweight: she names a gendered constraint, so the softness may be learned strategy. In the same episode she says 'I've always been able to make sure that I'm heard' (S59).

claims.claim: Her unnamed male co-star told the director: 'Don't do that, man. Don't put her through that.'
claims.passage: Her co-star intervened: "Don't do that, man. Don't put her through that."
claims.inference: Another person drew the line for her.
claims.alternative: Her account; co-star and film unnamed.

claims.claim: She said that if she had spoken up in the same way it 'wouldn't have been received well'.
claims.passage: the same words from her, she said, "wouldn't have been received well."
claims.inference: Gendered explanation in her words.
claims.alternative: Self-report.

claims.claim: Official Theroux clip: 'I've always been able to make sure that I'm heard.'
claims.passage: "I've always been able to make sure that I'm heard"
claims.inference: Counterweight to C23.

claims.inference: Discriminator 2.
claims.alternative: In the same segment she says she argued 'a lot' with directors early on and still does 'in a softer way'; the story mostly shows a gendered constraint she names.

claims.claim: Harper's Bazaar UK, April 2025: 'I've now come to terms with things that I don't like about myself and want to change. I don't want to have things just happen to me any more.'
claims.passage: "I don't want to have things just happen to me any more."
claims.inference: A wish to stop being carried by momentum.
claims.alternative: In context (S14) it follows 'I've worked back-to-back since I started, and I've missed so much' and is self-directed; it is used only in the change arc, not as defiance evidence.

claims.passage: Reports of tension with the director, Olivia Wilde, rested largely on anonymous sources, and in 2026 Wilde said, "I've never had a screaming match on my set."
claims.inference: Establishes that the feud narrative is disputed; nothing here establishes Pugh's behaviour.

claims.claim: British Vogue 2024: 'I am someone that loves falling in love. I love looking after people. I love caring for people. I love the feeling of someone being there.'
claims.passage: "I am someone that loves falling in love. I love looking after people. I love caring for people. I love the feeling of someone being there."
claims.inference: The strongest evidence for a caring/relational (Type 2) or security (Type 6) reading; 'people feel good in my presence' also fits a mood-keeper (Type 7).
claims.alternative: Wanting a home and family at 28-30 is common and life-stage driven. These statements come from interviews framed around a new relationship.

claims.claim: Ashley Park (Vanity Fair 2026): 'She's a great chef, she's a great host, she's a great designer, she's a great planner.'
claims.passage: "She's a great chef, she's a great host, she's a great designer, she's a great planner."

type_hypothesis.against: Type 8: four collaborators from 2019 to 2026 describe steel and an unapologetic presence (C57, C32, C83, C84); she calls herself 'a bit of a big mouth' (C03), argued 'a lot' with directors early on (C131), pushed Marvel and Braff past caution (C13, C85, C86), defended a partner and causes at real cost (C16, C88, C26, C90, C91, C92, C128), pre-empts shame by controlling exposure (C129, C154) and says she doesn't find it hard to talk about what doesn't sit right (C130). Her pushback defends autonomy and people she loves, which favors the Eight (C66, C156). Type 2: her costliest self-report is about hiding pain for others' sake (C09, C76, C94), she loves looking after people (C30) and is praised as a host (C106), though hosting is her family's trade (C31).
